context.objective: Document how we carry out Invoice approval and payment handoff, the controls and what needs confirmation.

turns.text: What starts this work?

This is invoice approval and payment handoff, also called AP invoice sign-off. The accounts payable manager is accountable from supplier receipt through Treasury's acceptance of the approved payment package. Treasury's payment execution is a separate process. The purpose is to send accurate, authorized supplier invoices to Treasury without paying the same invoice twice.
What event or incoming item starts the AP invoice sign-off work?

A supplier email to the shared AP mailbox starts a case. Each business day by 10 a.m. the AP analyst saves the invoice in the invoice folder and enters supplier, invoice number, amount and receipt date in the invoice register with status Received. The analyst uses the register to route the case into the duplicate check.
What does the duplicate check compare?

The AP analyst searches the invoice register for the same supplier and invoice number. A matching earlier invoice is a duplicate: the analyst links the two entries, sends the supplier a duplicate notice, marks the new entry Duplicate closed, and ends that case. If there is no match, the analyst marks it New and starts the purchase-order and receipt match.
What does the purchase-order and receipt match compare?

For a new invoice, the AP analyst compares supplier, amount and line items with the purchase order in the purchasing system and receipt in the receiving register. The analyst records the outcome in the invoice register. A complete match goes to the value decision. For a mismatch the analyst marks Hold and opens a case in the exception log, sends the buyer the difference, and follows up daily. The buyer obtains a corrected invoice or receiving record, records the resolution in the exception log, and returns it to AP. The analyst repeats the match before the hold is released.
How does the value decision determine what happens to a matched invoice?

The AP analyst checks the invoice value in the register. Below $50,000 the matched invoice goes directly to the department manager. At $50,000 or above, the controller first checks the matched package in the invoice folder and records an approve or reject decision in the approval register. A controller approval goes to the department manager; a controller rejection goes to the correction route. The approval matrix requires this threshold. This extra controller review adds one business day of staff effort, is included in the existing AP service with no separate charge, and remains mandatory for high-value invoices. Both routes are variations of the same invoice process.
What does the controller check in the matched package before recording approval or rejection?

The department manager reviews the matched invoice and purchase order from the invoice folder through the approval portal and records Approve or Reject. For either controller or manager rejection, the AP analyst records the reason in the exception log, sends it to the buyer, and sets status Correction required. The buyer resolves the reason with the supplier or receiving department and returns corrected documents to AP. The analyst then repeats the purchase-order and receipt match; the invoice follows the value and approval decisions again.
What does the department manager check before recording Approve or Reject?

After manager approval, the AP analyst saves the manager decision and any controller decision with the invoice and purchase order in the invoice folder, marks the register Ready for Treasury, and sends the package link through the Treasury queue. A Treasury analyst checks that the package link opens and records Accepted in the queue. AP marks the case Handed off and closes it when that acceptance is recorded. The package and register remain available as the handoff evidence.
What happens if Treasury rejects or delays the package?

The duplicate search, three-way match, value threshold and manager approval are required controls. The controller review is required at the high-value threshold. The AP analyst prepares the package, while the department manager approves it; the controller separately reviews high-value items. The register, exception log, approval register, portal decisions and Treasury acceptance provide the evidence for each check and handoff.
About how many invoices does AP normally process in a month?

The AP analyst checks open holds and rejections each business day. If a buyer has not supplied corrected material by the end of the second business day, the analyst escalates the exception log entry to the AP manager. The manager assigns a backup buyer and records the assignment in the log; the backup returns the correction to AP for the same recheck. Standard matched invoices target handoff within two business days, and high-value invoices target three business days.
About how many invoices does AP typically process each month?

The analyst copies invoice details from email into the register and follows up on exceptions manually. These activities consume about fifteen minutes of staff effort per invoice and are the main reported friction. Waiting for corrected documents is the main source of delay; the team tracks overdue cases in the exception log.
About how many invoices does AP typically process each month?

A duplicate payment can cause cash loss and recovery work. An incorrect or unapproved invoice can cause a supplier dispute or inaccurate payment. A late handoff can delay supplier payment. The AP manager reviews these risks with the team each month using the exception log.
What happens if Treasury cannot open the package link or does not record acceptance on time?

The AP operating procedure describes the steps and escalation. The invoice register template, exception log template, approval matrix, purchase order, receiving register, portal decision record and Treasury queue receipt document the work. The AP manager maintains the procedure and templates.
Does the AP operating procedure describe how this work is carried out today?

That covers the process from supplier email to Treasury acceptance, including duplicate closure, mismatch rework, the high-value approval route, manager rejection, escalation and the evidence retained. Treasury executes payment as a separate process.
Does the $50,000 approval threshold apply the same way across the entities or clients AP supports?
Your account so far is saved. 6 of 16 topics are complete and 10 are partly covered; the Notes list shows what is missing. You can create a draft from what is here, or keep answering.

topics.answer: Invoice approval and payment handoff, also called AP invoice sign-off, runs from supplier receipt through Treasury acceptance of the approved payment package; Treasury payment execution is a separate process.
Send accurate, authorized supplier invoices to Treasury without paying the same invoice twice.

A supplier email to the shared AP mailbox starts a case. Each business day by 10 a.m., the AP analyst saves and registers invoices. Handoff targets are two business days for standard matched invoices and three for high-value invoices; the event from which those targets are measured is UNKNOWN.

For the payment handoff, a Treasury analyst checks that the package link opens and records Accepted; AP marks the case Handed off and closes it. The package and register remain available as evidence. A duplicate case ends after the entries are linked, the supplier is notified and the new entry is marked Duplicate closed. Treasury payment execution is separate.
The accounts payable manager is accountable from supplier receipt through Treasury acceptance of the approved package.

The AP analyst saves and registers the invoice as Received, searches for a duplicate and either closes a matching case or marks it New. For a new invoice, the analyst compares supplier, amount and line items with the purchase order and receipt and records the outcome. A mismatch is held and logged, sent to the buyer and followed up daily; the buyer obtains and logs a correction and returns it for a repeat match before hold release. A complete match is routed by value: below $50,000 to the department manager, or at or above that amount first to the controller. Either approval rejection is logged and sent to the buyer for correction and a repeat match and approval route. After manager approval, AP saves the package and decisions, marks Ready for Treasury and sends the link; Treasury records acceptance and AP closes the case. Open holds and rejections are checked each business day; an overdue correction is escalated and a backup buyer returns it for recheck. Hold-release details and Treasury failure or delay handling remain UNKNOWN.

The participant identifies duplicate search, three-way match, value threshold and manager approval as required controls, with controller review at the high-value threshold. The analyst compares supplier, amount and line items to the purchase order and receipt; the controller checks the matched package and the manager reviews the invoice and purchase order, but their specific checks are UNKNOWN. The analyst prepares the package, the department manager approves it, and the controller separately reviews high-value items. Whether this role separation is formally or system-enforced is UNKNOWN. Rejections go for correction and the match and routing recur. Treasury checks that the link opens before acceptance. The register, exception log, approval register, portal decisions and Treasury acceptance are reported evidence. The AP manager reviews risks monthly using the exception log; the review's detailed actions and output are UNKNOWN. Client involvement remains unresolved.

The participant describes below-$50,000 direct manager routing and the $50,000-or-above controller-first route as variations of the same process. The participant attributes the threshold to the approval matrix. The extra controller review adds one business day of staff effort, has no separate charge and remains mandatory for high-value invoices. Standard matched and high-value handoff targets are two and three business days respectively. A mismatch follows a hold and correction route rather than the complete-match route. Applicability across entities and clients and other differences are UNKNOWN.

Manual copying from email into the register and manual exception follow-up are the main reported friction; together they take an estimated 15 minutes of staff effort per invoice. Waiting for corrected documents is the main source of delay. The high-value controller review adds one business day of staff effort.
Duplicate payment can cause cash loss and recovery work; an incorrect or unapproved invoice can cause a supplier dispute or inaccurate payment; late handoff can delay supplier payment.

The participant says the AP operating procedure describes the steps and escalation, and the AP manager maintains it and the templates. The invoice register and exception log templates, approval matrix, purchase order, receiving register, portal decision record and Treasury queue receipt document the work. The invoice folder, register, approval register and exception log also hold the described case records. These materials were not supplied for review; procedure and template access locations are UNKNOWN.

The reported boundary runs from supplier receipt through Treasury acceptance; Treasury payment execution is a separate process. Entity and client applicability, parent lifecycle and whether the account represents general GPFS practice are UNKNOWN.

A matching earlier supplier and invoice number is treated as a duplicate. A mismatch is held and corrected before a repeat match and hold release. The participant attributes the $50,000 controller-first threshold to the approval matrix; below it the invoice goes directly to the department manager. Rejections return for correction, match and renewed approval routing. AP escalates if corrected material is not supplied by the end of the second business day. The matrix was not supplied, and rule interpretation, conflicting sources, overrides and the escalation clock start are UNKNOWN.

Suppliers send invoice emails. AP uses purchase orders from the purchasing system and receipts from the receiving register. Buyers obtain and return corrections, including from suppliers or the receiving department for rejections. AP sends the approved package link to Treasury, which checks and accepts it; Treasury payment execution is separate. Broader upstream readiness and parallel-process relationships are UNKNOWN.

Supplier email enters the shared AP mailbox; the invoice is saved in the invoice folder and details are manually copied into the invoice register. Purchase orders are in the purchasing system and receipts in the receiving register. The invoice register holds match outcomes and statuses; the exception log holds mismatch and rejection information and backup assignments. The controller records decisions in the approval register, the manager uses the approval portal, and Treasury records acceptance in its queue. The authoritative record for each result and access or enforcement arrangements are UNKNOWN.

Typical invoice counts, peak volumes and exception rates are UNKNOWN. The participant estimates that copying invoice details and manually following up on exceptions together consume about 15 minutes of staff effort per invoice; the high-value review adds one business day of staff effort.
